analysis.one_liner: Protects workers from being fired for reporting workplace and public health-safety violations, with a uniform federal complaint system.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 45 House Democrats and a hearing in November 1989, never left committee and never got a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred employers from firing or punishing employees who report violations of federal health and safety laws, who testify in proceedings about such violations, or who refuse to take part in activities they reasonably believe are dangerous. It would have centralized all federal health-and-safety whistleblower complaints in a new office inside the Department of Labor, with a 180-day filing window, investigations within 60 days, an administrative hearing process, and remedies including reinstatement, back pay, and double damages for willful violations. It would have replaced the patchwork of separate whistleblower provisions scattered across more than a dozen existing federal laws with one uniform procedure.
analysis.who_benefits: Private-sector workers and job applicants who expose unsafe or unlawful practices would gain a single, faster, and stronger remedy than today's fragmented laws: an investigation within 60 days, a possible immediate reinstatement order that stays in effect while the case is litigated, reinstatement with back pay and benefits, consequential damages, double damages for willful disregard of public safety, and attorney's fees. The public also gains, because retaliation is a major reason workers stay silent about hazards, and final orders would be sent to the federal agency with jurisdiction so the underlying violation gets investigated.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and the public near hazards

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit employers from discharging or discriminating against any employee, former employee, or applicant who reports, intends to report, or participates in proceedings about violations of federal health or safety law, and would void agreements that waive those rights.

It would create an investigation office within the Department of Labor that must investigate complaints within 60 days and can issue preliminary orders for immediate reinstatement, which a request for a hearing would not pause.

Winning complainants could receive reinstatement with back pay and lost benefits, consequential damages, double damages for willful and wanton violations, abatement orders, and recovery of attorney's fees.
It would recognize the right of employees to refuse to work in conditions they reasonably believe pose a bona fide danger, provided they promptly report the danger to the employer.
Final orders would be referred to the federal agency with jurisdiction over the reported practice, which must take appropriate action and report back within 30 days.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who retaliate against health and safety whistleblowers would bear the cost: reinstatement, back pay, consequential and possibly double damages, and the complainant's legal fees, plus new posting requirements. Businesses generally would face a single federal complaint system applying to virtually all private employers engaged in interstate commerce, including state and local government employers, though the bill does not apply to deliberate violations an employee causes on their own.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose substantial new liability on employers, including double damages for willful violations and attorney's fees, and its protections turn on what the employee 'believes' rather than whether a violation is ultimately proven, which employers would argue invites costly claims.

A preliminary reinstatement order would take effect before any hearing and would not be paused by a request for a hearing, so an employer could be compelled to take back and pay an accused retaliator while the case is still being litigated.

The bill would supersede the enforcement procedures of the more than a dozen existing federal whistleblower laws, replacing specialized procedures that some agencies and employers may consider better tailored to their industries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and the public, the upside is strong: a uniform, time-limited, fee-supported path to report hazards without losing a livelihood, replacing a fragmented system the bill's findings describe as inadequate. The costs fall mainly on employers facing retaliation claims, and the strongest design concerns are the unrebuttable-by-delay preliminary reinstatement order and a subjective 'believes' standard, though the bill does include an exemption for employees who deliberately cause violations and a burden-shifting rule that protects employers who would have acted the same way anyway.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, got a subcommittee hearing in November 1989, and then sat without a markup or floor vote until the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. William D. Ford of Michigan introduced the bill on September 28, 1989, with 45 Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred jointly to the House Education and Labor Committee and the House Post Office and Civil Service Committee.
It was assigned to subcommittees in both committees, including Labor-Management Relations, Health and Safety, and Labor Standards, and a subcommittee hearing was held on November 16, 1989.
Executive comments were requested from OMB, OPM, the Postal Service, and the Mine Safety and Health Administration between October and December 1989.
No further action is recorded after December 14, 1989: the bill was never reported out of committee and never received a vote in either chamber before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that retaliated against health and safety whistleblowers continued operating under the older, fragmented protections without facing the bill's reinstatement, double-damage, and fee-shifting remedies. Workers and the public got nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers facing no new whistleblower liability

for.name: Rep. William D. Ford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 45 cosponsors for it.

for.name: 45 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 45 recorded cosponsors were Democrats.

for.role: Subcommittees on Labor-Management Relations, Health and Safety, and Labor Standards
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on November 16, 1989.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Rep. Augustus Hawkins, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee; no markup or floor action followed the November 1989 hearing.

against.name: House Post Office and Civil Service Committee
against.role: Second committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Postal Personnel and Modernization Subcommittee in October 1989 and took no further recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 cosponsors were House Democrats, but no vote was ever taken, so the record shows a Democratic sponsorship base rather than a recorded partisan split on the merits.

industries.industry: Private employers across industries (manufacturing, mining, transport, energy, and other regulated workplaces)
industries.note: The bill would have made firing or punishing employees for reporting federal health and safety violations costly, with reinstatement, back pay, double damages for willful violations, and fee-shifting. Its defeat left those employers under the weaker, patchwork protections that already existed.

industries.industry: Federal and state workplace-safety enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would route whistleblower complaints and final orders through the Department of Labor and refer violations to the responsible agency for action, adding caseload but giving agencies a new enforcement pipeline. The record shows agencies were asked for comment but the bill died before any agency position mattered.
